title: Non-verbal Reasoning
relevance: Hardware and general-aptitude OAs test spatial working memory with figure series, analogies, mirror/water images, counting, folding, and Raven's-matrix completion under tight time pressure.
company_notes: Raven's-matrix pattern completion appears on inductive-reasoning assessments used by SHL, AMCAT, and CoCubes; similar figure items appear on hardware and general-aptitude OAs.

phases.goal: Establish that non-verbal items are about spotting one consistent figure transformation and naming the four that cover almost every item.

must_hit.point: Non-verbal items give figures, not words: a pattern is transformed step by step and you predict, complete, or classify it by spotting one consistent transformation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says the skill is identifying a single rule—rotation, reflection, count change, or position shift—and applying it, not reading verbal logic.

must_hit.point: The four transformations that explain almost every figure item are rotation (fixed angle, same direction each step), reflection (flip across a line), count change (dots/sides/lines increase or decrease by a fixed amount), and position shift (an element moves a fixed step).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists all four and notes you should test them in order until one fits.

must_hit.point: A mirror image is reflection across a vertical line (left↔right); a water image is reflection across a horizontal line at the base (top↔bottom).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Clearly separates vertical flip (mirror) from horizontal flip (water) without calling either a rotation.

probes: What are the four transformations you should try first on a non-verbal figure item?
How does a mirror image differ from a water image?

hints.1: Think about what kinds of single rules can turn one figure into the next.
hints.2: Name rotate, reflect, count, and shift; then define mirror as left↔right and water as top↔bottom.
hints.3: Almost every item is one of: fixed-angle rotation, line reflection, fixed count change, or fixed position shift; mirror flips left↔right, water flips top↔bottom.

phases.goal: Show how to apply series, analogy, classification, counting, folding, matrix, embedded, dot, grouping, and rule-detection procedures mechanically.

must_hit.point: In a figure series, when the pattern is confusing, count something numeric—sides, dots, line segments, or rotation angle—and check for an arithmetic step such as a steady +1 or a fixed-angle turn.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions counting a quantity or angle across frames and predicting the next value, e.g. sides 3→4→5→6 so next is seven, or arrow 45° clockwise each step.

must_hit.point: In a figure analogy, find the transformation from A to B and apply that identical transformation to C.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says A→B is the rule (e.g. 90° clockwise), then applies the same turn to C rather than inventing a new rule.

must_hit.point: When counting figures in a composite drawing, count systematically by size (small then large), never at random; for a grid of cells, rectangles equal choosing 2 of the vertical lines times 2 of the horizontal lines.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes size-class counting and/or the line-pair rule, e.g. 4 small + 4 large triangles = 8, or binom on the three vertical and three horizontal lines giving 9 rectangles.

must_hit.point: In paper folding and punching, punched holes reappear mirrored across every fold line; each fold doubles the holes by reflecting them across that crease.
must_hit.evidence_hint: After a right-onto-left fold and one punch, expects two holes symmetric about the vertical centre line on unfold.

probes: Walk through how you would continue a figure series or complete an A:B :: C:? analogy.
How do you count triangles or rectangles in a composite figure, and what happens to punched holes when you unfold a folded sheet?

hints.1: Separate series (continue the rule) from analogy (copy A→B onto C).
hints.2: For counting, group by size or use line pairs on a grid; for folding, reflect the hole across each crease.
hints.3: Series: arithmetic count or fixed turn; analogy: same transform on C; counting: small+large or choose 2 lines each way; folding: each fold mirrors and doubles holes.

phases.goal: Distinguish reflection from rotation, mirror from water, and visual hunting from mechanical counting under OA time pressure.

must_hit.point: A reflection is not a rotation: a chiral shape with no symmetry that has been flipped can never be recreated by turning the original—handedness, not just orientation, must be checked.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States that the mirrored odd-one-out cannot be produced by any rotation of the others, even if it looks merely tilted.

must_hit.point: Quick test for mirror vs water: in a mirror image left/right swap while up/down stay; in a water image up/down swap while left/right stay—tracking one directional feature avoids confusing either with a 180° rotation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses one pointing feature (e.g. flag direction and base) to reject a 180° rotation distractor for water or an unchanged/rotated option for mirror.

must_hit.point: For grids, do not hunt visually—use the counting rule; the reliable OA method is mechanical (name rotate/reflect/count/shift and apply once), not artistic intuition, under about a minute or less per figure.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Prefers the binom/line-pair or size-class method and naming a single transformation over eyeballing under time pressure.

probes: When classifying odd-one-out figures, how do you tell a rotation of the same shape from a reflection?
How do you keep mirror images, water images, and 180° rotations straight?

hints.1: Ask whether turning alone could produce the figure, or whether left/right vs up/down flipped.
hints.2: Check handedness for odd-one-out; for mirror/water track one directional feature and keep the other axis fixed.
hints.3: Mirrored chiral figure ≠ any rotation; mirror swaps left↔right only; water swaps top↔bottom only; 180° rotation changes both axes and is a common trap.

phases.goal: Apply the mechanical checklist to the main OA item types: matrix completion, embedded figures, dot regions, grouping, and stated-rule checks.

must_hit.point: In a 3×3 figure matrix (Raven's format), find the rule across rows and down columns—e.g. a quantity that rises by one moving right and moving down—and fill the blank cell that continues it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Reads a pattern like rows 1,2,3 / 2,3,4 / 3,4,? and supplies the next count (5 dots) rather than guessing from appearance alone.

must_hit.point: An embedded figure must appear at the same size, orientation, and proportion; a rotated or mirror-flipped copy does not count.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects an inverted chevron (∨) when the target is an upward ∧, and accepts only the option containing that exact pair of strokes.

must_hit.point: In a dot situation, track membership for each overlapping shape (inside/outside) and pick the option with the same region; for grouping, split by a hidden shared property such as straight-edged vs curved; for rule detection, check the stated numeric rule figure by figure.
must_hit.evidence_hint: E.g. inside triangle and circle but outside square; groups (1,3,5) straight vs (2,4,6) curved; or dots equal sides only on the matching polygon.

probes: How would you complete a 3×3 Raven's-style matrix of figures?
What must be true for a figure to count as containing an embedded target, and how do you solve a dot-region or grouping item?

hints.1: Look for a row/column progression, then for exact containment or region membership.
hints.2: Matrix: same increment across and down; embedded: same size/orientation; dot: list inside/outside for each shape.
hints.3: Continue the matrix count rule into the blank; reject reflected/rotated embeds; match all overlap constraints; group by the shared property or verify the stated rule.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: A flipped chiral figure cannot be obtained by any rotation of the original; odd-one-out and mirror-image items hinge on handedness, so a 90°-rotated member still belongs while the mirrored one is the outsider.
Mirror flips left↔right with up/down unchanged; water flips top↔bottom with left/right unchanged. A 180° rotation changes both axes and is the standard distractor for both.
Counting by size class or by choosing pairs of grid lines beats eyeballing composites; for an m×n cell grid, rectangles are binom(m+1,2)×binom(n+1,2), so a 2×2 grid yields 9.

tradeoffs.topic: Mechanical transformation naming vs artistic intuition
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Under a minute or less per figure on hardware/aptitude OAs, name the single transformation (rotate/reflect/count/shift), apply it once, and for folding remember each fold doubles holes by reflecting across the crease—rather than relying on visual guesswork.

gotchas.trap: Treating a reflection as if it were a rotation, or picking the figure that merely looks tilted differently as the odd one out.
gotchas.correction: A mirrored chiral shape can never be recreated by turning; the outsider is the one whose handedness differs, while a 90°-rotated figure still belongs to the group.

gotchas.trap: Confusing a water image with a 180° rotation (e.g. flag ends up pointing the wrong way).
gotchas.correction: Water keeps left/right and only swaps top/bottom; track one directional feature so the base-at-top, still-pointing-the-same-way image wins over the rotated distractor.

gotchas.trap: Confusing a mirror image with an unchanged figure, a 180° rotation, or a water image.
gotchas.correction: Mirror flips left↔right only; base stays at the bottom while left/right pointing reverses—unchanged, 180°-rotated, and top↔bottom options are wrong.

gotchas.trap: When counting triangles, missing the inverted middle triangle or the large outer triangle; when counting squares, forgetting the outer square.
gotchas.correction: Count by size: e.g. 4 small + 4 large = 8 in the diagonals square; 4 small + 1 outer = 5 squares; midpoint triangle figure is 4 small + 1 large = 5.

gotchas.trap: On unfold after a single vertical fold punch, forgetting the second layer or mirroring across the wrong axis.
gotchas.correction: The punch goes through both layers, so unfolding yields two holes symmetric about the vertical fold (centre line), not one hole, a horizontal mirror, or invented extras.

gotchas.trap: Accepting a rotated or mirror-flipped copy as an embedded figure (e.g. inverted ∨ for target ∧).
gotchas.correction: The embedded target must match at the same size, orientation, and proportion; reflection or rotation is the standard distractor and does not count.
